paras: The lynching of Henry Jessies, a Black man also reported as Henry Jessee and as John Jones, took place near Dickinsonville in Russell County, Virginia, on the night of Saturday, August 2, 1890, when a posse of about a hundred men hanged him from a tree and shot his body. He was accused of sexually assaulting a white woman that afternoon, and one account said his body was found the next day with thirty-six bullet holes. Virginia papers reported the killing under headlines calling him a "negro fiend," while a Roanoke dispatch noted that his brother claimed he could identify the lynchers.

According to the Abingdon correspondent of the Richmond Dispatch, the accused man had only recently returned from the penitentiary, where he had served a term for forgery. The same Dispatch correspondent called him "dissolute and desperate," a description that came from the white writer alone.

The Dispatch correspondence said that about 4 o'clock on Saturday afternoon the man entered the yard of a farmer near Dickinsonville, where the farmer's two daughters were standing, and that both screamed and fled when he tried to grasp one of them. By this account he then went into the house, assaulted the mother, described as "quite an old woman," and escaped to the wooded hills. Other reports named the woman as the wife of John W. Gibson and placed the assault near Old Court House or Russell Court-house.

The Dispatch reported that a posse of a hundred men captured him that night, that he was "identified," and that he was then hanged from a tree and his body riddled with bullets. A shorter account printed in the Evening Star and the Staunton Spectator said instead that he was arrested that evening and given a preliminary trial before a justice of the peace before being hanged that night. In that version his body was found still hanging the following day with thirty-six bullet holes in it.

A Roanoke telegram to the Richmond Dispatch, dated August 6, reported that the dead man had a brother in that city who said "he can spot the lynchers" and threatened to "make it lively for them." The Abingdon correspondent, by contrast, wrote that the community was "still very much enraged over the action of this fiend," meaning the accused man rather than his killers. No report of an inquest, of arrests of the lynchers, or of grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The story ran only in white papers, mostly in Virginia, between August 7 and August 15, 1890, and no account in the Black press has been found. The Richmond Dispatch published the Abingdon correspondence on August 7 under the subheads "A Negro Fiend Lynched in Russell County" and "A NEGRO LYNCHED," below a report on the federal court term at Abingdon. The same issue carried the Roanoke item under the heading "KNOWS THE LYNCHERS," naming the man John Jones and calling him "the negro fiend." That day the Alexandria Gazette reduced the news to a single line in its "Virginia News" column, worded almost exactly like the Dispatch's opening sentence.

The Evening Star printed the version naming "Henry Jessee" on August 8, and the Staunton Spectator ran it without his name on August 13 under the heading "A NEGRO FIEND LYNCHED." The Clarke Courier of Berryville and the Shenandoah Herald of Woodstock reprinted these items on August 14 and 15. Every account stated the accusation as fact, with words such as "outraged" and "assaulted," and none questioned the hanging; the only objection to the lynchers came from the brother, reported secondhand from Roanoke.

The man's name appears as Henry Jessies in the Abingdon correspondence, Henry Jessee in the Evening Star, and John Jones in the Roanoke telegram, though all three describe the same accusation in the same county. The accounts also differ on whether he was seized by a pursuing posse and hanged once identified, or was first arrested and examined before a justice of the peace. The Abingdon letter, written nearest the scene, gives the fuller narrative but mentions no hearing, while the shorter version does not say how the prisoner passed from the justice to the men who hanged him.

accounts.label: Roanoke telegram
accounts.gist: John Jones, who assaulted Mrs. J. W. Gibson near Russell Court-house, was hanged by a mob; his brother says he can identify the lynchers.

accounts.label: Short state-news version
accounts.gist: He outraged John W. Gibson's wife near Old Court House, was arrested, had a preliminary trial before a justice of the peace, and was hanged that night; found next day with 36 bullet holes.

framing.detail: Richmond Dispatch headed it 'A Negro Fiend Lynched in Russell County', called him 'dissolute and desperate' and reported the community 'very much enraged' at him, not at the lynchers.
The Roanoke item 'KNOWS THE LYNCHERS' called him 'the negro fiend' but reported his brother's threat against the lynchers.
Alexandria Gazette gave a single line in 'Virginia News'.
Staunton Spectator headed it 'A NEGRO FIEND LYNCHED' and stated the outrage as fact.
Evening Star and the Clarke Courier and Shenandoah Herald ran the short version without comment.
